title: Introduction to AngularJS
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and boundary of introduction to angularjs in an AngularJS 1.x application.
Apply at least one relevant API or practice from introduction to angularjs to a small example.

content.intro: Use introduction to angularjs in the context of an existing AngularJS 1.x codebase. Identify the inputs, observable UI or API behavior, version constraints and cleanup requirements; then verify the behavior with a repeatable local test.
content.why_it_matters: Introduction to AngularJS helps maintain an existing AngularJS application without mixing API assumptions, UI behavior and operational risks.

items.title: Assuming the framework version
items.text: Read package manifests and lockfiles before applying a documented API; record version-specific differences.

items.title: Mixing concerns
items.text: Keep view state, data-access logic and security decisions in their appropriate layers.

items.title: Testing only the happy path
items.text: Include empty, invalid, failed-request or teardown behavior where it applies.

content.task: Build a tiny local example that demonstrates introduction to angularjs. Include a normal case and a relevant edge/failure/cleanup case, then record the expected result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the target behavior and uses the API documented for the application version.
The normal and edge/failure/cleanup behaviors can be repeated with documented steps.
No client-only authorization or unsafe untrusted-HTML assumptions are introduced.
hints: Start with the smallest observable behavior, then add the supporting controller, component, directive, service or route only if needed.
Read the actual package lockfile and API contract before applying a code pattern.
Use browser console/network evidence and a regression test rather than guessing.
content.solution_notes: Use the reference snippet as a starting point, not a complete production implementation. Keep the code in the correct layer, test a failure path, and document any compatibility or security trade-off.
summary: Explain what Introduction to AngularJS owns and the boundary it should not cross.
Verify the normal case and at least one relevant edge/error/cleanup case.
Keep the exact AngularJS version, security, accessibility and maintenance constraints visible.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the AngularJS version or API behavior
common_mistakes.why: Legacy applications may use different 1.x versions and old third-party modules.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the lockfile/package manifest and version-specific official reference before editing.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing view, data and authorization responsibilities
common_mistakes.why: It makes behavior difficult to test and can incorrectly treat client checks as security boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep reusable data access in services and enforce permissions/validation on the server.

common_mistakes.why: Empty results, request rejection, invalid input or scope teardown may behave differently.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a repeatable edge/error/cleanup check and retain it as a regression test.

how_to_run: Use the existing project setup and pinned framework version.
Serve browser-based examples over HTTP rather than opening files directly when route/template loading requires it.
Use the project test runner for automated tests; do not execute arbitrary learner code in the API server.
troubleshooting: Check the browser console for module/provider/template errors.
Check the network panel for failed script, template and API requests.
Compare the failing behavior with a minimal example and add a regression test after the repair.
content.accessibility_notes: Use semantic HTML, keyboard-operable controls, accessible names, visible focus, and status/error messages that do not rely on color alone.
content.version_notes: AngularJS is end-of-support. Confirm the application’s exact 1.x version and dependency lockfile before using an API or changing a package.
